title: When the Rate Runs Out of Room

steps.body:
Exponential growth is a lie told about the short term. Nothing grows forever — food runs out, space runs out.

So make k **stop being constant**. Let it shrink to zero as the population approaches a ceiling K:

**dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K)**

When P is small the bracket is nearly 1 and growth is nearly exponential. When P nears K the bracket goes to zero and growth stops. **The logistic equation is what happens when k stops being constant.**
Every curve runs to the same ceiling.

widget.prompt: dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4). Drag the starting value to the ceiling itself — the one curve that never moves.
widget.successFeedback: P = 4, the carrying capacity, where every segment is flat. Now drag away: from below the curve climbs to 4 in an S-shape; from ABOVE it falls to 4. Every solution ends in the same place. The ceiling is not something the model was told about — it is a consequence of the bracket (1 − P/K) shutting the growth down.
widget.lowFeedback: Below the ceiling — the curve is climbing toward it, and it will not stop until it arrives.
widget.highFeedback: Above the ceiling — too many for the food supply, so the population FALLS back to it.

cml.actionGoal: Change an initial condition and trace a solution that remains tangent to the local direction field.

predict.prompt: dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4). Start a population exactly at 4 — the carrying capacity. Over time it will…

options.label: Creep above 4, since it is still growing

predict.reveal: It never moves. At P = 4 the factor (1 − P/4) is exactly zero, so the whole rate is zero — a row of perfectly flat slope marks. Equilibrium is not growth that has become slow; it is growth that has become nothing, and the equation says so before any curve is drawn.

widget.prompt: dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4). Drag the starting value down to 1 — far under the ceiling — and look at the shape of the curve's first stretch.
widget.successFeedback: From P = 1 the first stretch is an almost pure exponential arc. With P well under 4 the bracket (1 − P/4) sits near 1, so the rate is close to plain 1.8P; the bend only arrives once the ceiling is within reach.
widget.lowFeedback: At 0 there is nothing to grow from at all, and the curve never leaves the axis. Come back up to 1, a small but real population.
widget.highFeedback: Above 1 the population is already a noticeable fraction of the ceiling, so the bracket has begun to bite and the curve bends sooner. Drag down to 1.

explanationVariants: When P is far below K, the bracket (1 − P/K) is close to 1, so dP/dt ≈ kP — ordinary exponential growth. The ceiling only bites when you get near it.
That is why the early stage of an epidemic, or of a species colonising an island, looks exponential.

widget.prompt: In dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K), what happens when P is very small compared with K?

options.label: Growth is nearly exponential because 1 − P/K is close to 1.
options.feedback: Right, and that is why the early stage of any logistic process looks exponential. The ceiling only makes itself felt as you approach it.

options.label: Growth stops because a very small P makes the rate zero.
options.feedback: Growth stops at the CEILING, not at the floor. A small population has plenty of room and grows nearly unchecked.

options.label: Population falls because a small P makes the bracket negative.
options.feedback: For 0 < P < K both factors are positive, so dP/dt > 0 — the population grows.

options.label: Growth is linear because kP has no exponential behavior.
options.feedback: With the bracket close to 1, the equation is essentially dP/dt = kP — proportional growth, which is exponential, not linear.

steps.body: The inflection point has a meaning.
explanationVariants: The growth RATE kP(1 − P/K) is a downward parabola in P with roots 0 and K, so it peaks at P = K/2 — half the ceiling.
That is the inflection point of the S-curve: the moment the growth stops accelerating and starts easing off.

widget.prompt: dP/dt = 1.8P(1 − P/4). At what population is the growth rate FASTEST?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ceiling, where growth has stopped completely. The fastest growth is at HALF of it.
An empty population grows at zero. The rate peaks in the middle: P = K/2 = 2.
That is the rate constant k, not a population. The rate is a downward parabola with roots 0 and 4, so it peaks at 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The rate is a downward parabola with roots 0 and 4: it peaks at P = 2, exactly half the carrying capacity.

steps.body:
So the logistic curve has a shape you can now read entirely off the equation:

**Below K/2** — growing, and growing FASTER. (concave up)
**At K/2** — the inflection: fastest growth, and the moment it starts easing.
**Above K/2** — still growing, but slowing. (concave down)
**At K** — stopped.

An S-curve, and every feature of it is forced by kP(1 − P/K).

explanationVariants: Between K/2 and K the population is still growing (dP/dt > 0) but the rate is falling — so the curve is concave down, easing toward the ceiling.
Growing and slowing at the same time: that is the top half of every S-curve, and it is what makes it an S.

widget.prompt: A logistic population sits between K/2 and K. What is it doing?

options.label: Growing more slowly because it is approaching K from below.
options.feedback: Right: dP/dt is still positive but shrinking. Growing and slowing at once, which is the top half of the S.

options.label: Shrinking because values above K/2 always decrease to zero.
options.feedback: Below the ceiling both factors are positive, so the population is still growing. It only shrinks if it somehow overshoots K.

options.label: Growing faster because the rate rises as P nears K.
options.feedback: That is the BOTTOM half, below K/2. Past the inflection, the growth rate is falling.

options.label: Holding steady because every value below K is equilibrium.
options.feedback: It holds steady only AT the ceiling. Between K/2 and K it is still climbing, just less and less eagerly.

steps.body: Read the long run, and the middle.
hints: The carrying capacity is where the bracket vanishes: 1 − P/500 = 0.
So K = 500, and the fastest growth is at half of that.
The question asks for the population at the inflection point.
explanationVariants: K = 500, so growth is fastest at P = 250 — half the carrying capacity.
And that is the practical use of the model: it tells a fishery or an epidemic where the turning point is, before it arrives.

widget.prompt: dP/dt = 0.3P(1 − P/500). At what population is growth fastest?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the carrying capacity K, where growth STOPS. The fastest growth is at K/2 = 250.
That is the rate constant k, not a population.
Half of the carrying capacity is 250, not 150. Read K from the bracket: 1 − P/500 = 0 gives K = 500.

widget.fallbackFeedback: K = 500, so the growth rate peaks at K/2 = 250.

steps.body: What happens when k stops being constant.
takeaways: dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K): nearly exponential when P is small, stopping dead at the ceiling K.
Equilibria at 0 (unstable) and K (stable). Every positive solution runs to K, from above or below.
The inflection sits at K/2 — the fastest growth is at HALF the carrying capacity, not at the top.
steps.teaser: Last chapter: what to do when the equation cannot be solved at all.

concept.body: Read the bracket. **(1 − P/K)** is nearly 1 when P is small (so growth is nearly exponential) and nearly 0 when P nears K (so growth shuts down). The bracket is the ceiling, written as algebra.

explanationVariants: The bracket vanishes when P = 800, so the carrying capacity is 800.

widget.prompt: dP/dt = 0.4P(1 − P/800). What is the carrying capacity?

commonErrors.feedback: That is where growth is FASTEST (half the ceiling). The ceiling itself is where the bracket vanishes: P = 800.
That is the rate constant k, not a population.
